content: The studies reviewed here provide detailed insights into the effects of antimalarial interventions and mass drug administration (MDA) on various health outcomes. 1. Antimalarial Therapy and All-Cause Mortality: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with follow-up periods ranging from 2 to 26 weeks suggest that therapeutic courses of antimalarial medications likely reduce all-cause mortality. However, the effect size varies, and it is possible that the intervention has little to no impact on overall mortality rates. The evidence is of moderate certainty due to serious imprecision. 2. Antimalarial Therapy and All-Cause Re-Admission During the Intervention Period: Based on data from 682 participants across three RCTs with follow-up periods of 2 to 14 weeks, antimalarial therapy likely decreases all-cause re-admissions during the intervention period. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious inconsistency. 3. Antimalarial Therapy and All-Cause Re-Admission Post-Intervention: Data from 558 participants in two RCTs with follow-up periods of 15 to 26 weeks indicate that antimalarial therapy likely results in little to no difference in all-cause re-admissions after the intervention period. The evidence is of moderate certainty due to serious imprecision. 4. Antimalarial Therapy and Severe Anemia Re-Admission During the Intervention Period: Evidence from 5,481 participants in three RCTs with follow-up periods of 2 to 14 weeks suggests that antimalarial therapy likely reduces severe anemia re-admissions during the intervention period. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious inconsistency. 5. Antimalarial Therapy and Severe Anemia Re-Admission Post-Intervention: Data from 558 participants in two RCTs with follow-up periods of 15 to 26 weeks indicate that antimalarial therapy likely reduces severe anemia re-admissions after the intervention period. The evidence is of moderate certainty due to serious imprecision. 6. Antimalarial Therapy and Severe Malaria Re-Admission Post-Intervention: Based on data from 470 participants in two RCTs with follow-up periods of 2 to 14 weeks, antimalarial therapy likely results in little to no difference in severe malaria re-admissions after the intervention period. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious imprecision. 7. Antimalarial Therapy and Clinical Malaria During the Intervention Period: Data from 3,356 participants in three RCTs with follow-up periods of 2 to 14 weeks suggest that antimalarial therapy likely reduces clinical malaria during the intervention period. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious inconsistency. 8. Antimalarial Therapy and Clinical Malaria Post-Intervention: Evidence from 3,325 participants in three RCTs with follow-up periods of 15 to 26 weeks indicates that antimalarial therapy likely results in little to no difference in clinical malaria after the intervention period. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious imprecision. 9. Antimalarial Therapy and Combined Clinical Malaria (Intervention + Post-Intervention Periods): Data from 3,387 participants in three RCTs with follow-up periods of 2 to 26 weeks suggest that antimalarial therapy likely reduces clinical malaria when considering both the intervention and post-intervention periods. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious inconsistency. 10. Drug-Related Adverse Events (Safety): Antimalarial therapy appears to result in little to no difference in the risk of drug-related adverse events. Most adverse events reported were minor, and no participants discontinued the study medication due to adverse effects. QTc prolongation events (measured using Fridericia’s correction) were asymptomatic, and no QTc values exceeded 500 ms. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious indirectness. 11. Mass Drug Administration (MDA) and Clinical Malaria Incidence in Moderate to High Transmission Areas (1–3 Months Post-MDA): MDA may reduce clinical malaria incidence in areas with moderate to high malaria transmission within 1–3 months post-MDA. However, the certainty of evidence is low due to very serious imprecision. 12. MDA and Clinical Malaria Incidence in Low to Very Low Transmission Areas (1–3 Months Post-MDA): MDA may reduce clinical malaria incidence in areas with low to very low malaria transmission within 1–3 months post-MDA. The certainty of evidence is low due to very serious imprecision. 13. MDA and Clinical Malaria Incidence in Low to Very Low Transmission Areas (4–12 Months Post-MDA): The effect of MDA on clinical malaria incidence in low to very low transmission areas 4–12 months post-MDA is uncertain. The certainty of evidence is very low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 14. MDA and P. vivax Clinical Malaria Incidence (4–12 Months Post-MDA): The impact of MDA on P. vivax clinical malaria incidence 4–12 months post-MDA is uncertain. The certainty of evidence is very low due to serious risk of bias and inconsistency. 15. MDA and P. falciparum Parasite Prevalence in Moderate to High Transmission Areas (4–12 Months Post-MDA): MDA may slightly increase P. falciparum parasite prevalence in moderate to high transmission areas 4–12 months post-MDA. The certainty of evidence is low due to very serious imprecision. 16. MDA and P. falciparum Parasite Prevalence in Low to Very Low Transmission Areas (<1 Month Post-MDA): MDA likely reduces P. falciparum parasite prevalence in low to very low transmission areas within 1 month post-MDA. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious risk of bias. 17. MDA and All-Cause Mortality in All Ages (<1 Month Post-MDA): The effect of MDA on all-cause mortality in all ages within 1 month post-MDA is uncertain. The certainty of evidence is very low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 18. MDA and All-Cause Mortality in Children Under 5 Years (<1 Month Post-MDA): The impact of MDA on all-cause mortality in children under 5 years within 1 month post-MDA is uncertain. The certainty of evidence is very low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 19. MDA and P. falciparum Parasite Prevalence in Low to Very Low Transmission Areas (1–3 Months Post-MDA): MDA likely reduces P. falciparum parasite prevalence in low to very low transmission areas within 1–3 months post-MDA. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious risk of bias. 20. MDA and P. falciparum Parasite Prevalence in Low to Very Low Transmission Areas (12–24 Months Post-MDA): The effect of MDA on P. falciparum parasite prevalence in low to very low transmission areas 12–24 months post-MDA is uncertain. The certainty of evidence is very low due to serious risk of bias and indirectness. These findings highlight the potential benefits and limitations of antimalarial therapies and MDA in reducing malaria-related outcomes, with varying levels of certainty depending on the context and study design.
